title: Bot Overlords, Deepfakes, and the Weight of the Robe — Judge Scott Schlegel on AI in the Courts (The Geek in Review)
pub: The Geek in Review / 3 Geeks and a Law Blog (hosts Greg Lambert & Marlene Gebauer)
author: Scott Schlegel

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Court AI: Existing failures set the comparison
st.an: Schlegel supports public-facing court AI while materially extending the cluster’s proposition: meaningful gains depend on funded legal technologists and redesigning case-management workflows, not merely deploying standalone drafting or research tools. He also grounds that approach in current budget and technical-capacity constraints, while treating projected timeline reductions as aspirations rather than measured outcomes.
qs: But the real magic is going to be when we are able to redesign our case management systems that does  heck of lot of things beforehand so that when we get the record, we have the record in a digestible format where we can shrink that six month timeline to six weeks.

So, you know, on-prem solutions, but  I don’t know that many judges know the difference between on-prem and off-prem, and we certainly don’t have the budgets for legal technologists to come in and build on-prem tools at the moment.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Schlegel accepts the cluster’s human-led, selective-deployment model and materially extends it to courts through a firm prohibition on delegating judicial decisions, practical chamber guidance, security controls, early disclosure rules and small pilots. His contribution is primarily an implementation framework for high-stakes judicial settings rather than evidence about general capability.
qs: So never turn over the judicial authority or the judicial decision-making to the bot overlords.
So, you know, always start small and start with a pilot.

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: The source supports shifting procurement from product claims toward structured buyer evaluation of strategic fit, real workflow use cases, integration and security. It provides practitioner guidance rather than quantitative evidence that these practices improve adoption or realized value.
qs: This seems logical, but be ready to talk about who your clients are, have some references, and demonstrate that you understand the buyer’s strategic challenges, not just your tech.
show real use cases that show how people are using your platform today to solve their business issues.

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: Schlegel supports the cluster’s emphasis on selective, contextual learning and retained professional judgment. He combines informal monitoring with established institutional resources and treats AI as a useful tool that must remain subordinate to judicial decision-making. His comments are normative and experiential rather than empirical.
qs: But I mean, look, formal resources, you’ve got the National Center for State Courts, you’ve got the Sedona Conference, you’ve got Bolch Institute.

st.t: Court responsibility: AI requires lifecycle supervision
st.an: Schlegel directly supports the cluster’s central proposition that AI may assist judicial work but cannot receive delegated judicial authority. He places human judgment and responsibility with the judge and grounds that boundary in the social contract and the stakes for litigants.
qs: And the first overview or the first statement that we try and make is that the judicial authority exists in the judicial officer, not the AI bot.

Marlene Gebauer (07:04)  Thank  Judge Scott Schlegel (07:09)  So if you’re gonna use these tools, it is about human judgment first and foremost and owning the responsibilities necessary to use these tools.

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: Schlegel directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition that technology’s operational benefits depend on organisational adaptation. He expects tools to help courts but makes foundational process reform and difficult change management prerequisites, while offering expectations and implementation guidance rather than measured outcomes.
qs: We’re much further  ahead and it’s not that simple to make these changes.

kp.k: Judicial authority must remain human despite AI assistance
kp.d: Schlegel describes short, nontechnical Sedona Conference guidelines for judges and clerks whose central principle is that judicial authority cannot be delegated to AI. He supports tools that improve efficiency while rejecting model-dependent adjudication, using custody decisions as a hypothetical example of unacceptable delegation. Reducing a six-month process to six weeks is an illustrative aspiration, not a measured outcome.
qs: the judicial authority exists in the judicial officer, not the AI bot. Full stop.
So never turn over the judicial authority or the judicial decision-making to the bot overlords.
that doesn’t mean we shouldn’t be using these tools to make us more efficient, effective so that we take maybe a six month process down to six weeks

kp.k: Competence and structured guidance underpin responsible judicial drafting
kp.d: Schlegel attributes continuing hallucinations in pleadings to inadequate competence with tools. Assuming rather than establishing that judges already use general-purpose LLMs to draft orders and opinions, he developed a ten-step responsible-use guide with sample prompts. He expects experienced users eventually to need fewer explicit steps. He reports positive feedback from readers but explicitly does not claim widespread judicial adoption.
qs: I think that’s an unfortunate reality based upon people, you know, not becoming competent with the tools.
So I just assumed that judges are starting to use it to draft orders and to draft opinions.
I really just tell everybody it’s a 10 step process.
So I don’t see wide adoption by every judge and judicial officer across the country, but those who have read it have been very positive.

kp.k: Judges should direct drafting rather than solicit independent decisions
kp.d: Schlegel distinguishes short writ dispositions from lengthy appellate opinions, judging current context windows inadequate for a 30-page appellate opinion. For bounded drafting, he recommends supplying the relevant law, facts and answer rather than asking an LLM to derive a first draft from parties’ submissions. This is his task-specific recommendation for assistance, not an empirical model-performance finding.
qs: I’m not going to use it to draft a 30 page appeal, opinion to an appeal because the context windows are not good enough yet.
Here’s the relevant facts. Here are the relevant. Here’s the answer. Here’s everything.
But never say, here are the briefs and the pleadings from the parties, give me a first draft.

kp.k: AI agreeableness risks reinforcing judges’ initial assumptions
kp.d: Schlegel distinguishes confirmation bias from general claims about model bias: systems that please users can strengthen an advocate’s preferred argument but improperly steer judicial reasoning. He describes an 'AI alignment test' in his guide intended to ensure the judge directs the reasoning rather than follows persuasive AI output. He also argues that model designers’ biases do not carry the democratic authority of elected judges.
qs: I’m talking about the confirmation bias where I always say that the LLMs are a man’s best friend today.
It wants to tell you what you want to hear.
one of the steps in my guide is what I call AI alignment test.
making sure that you are the one directing the path as opposed to being led down the path by the AI because it is so convincing and so good now.

kp.k: Budgets, procurement and trusted platforms condition court adoption
kp.d: Schlegel reports that courts lack budgets for technologists to build on-premises systems and often cannot afford enterprise minimum-user requirements. He predicts greater adoption as AI enters familiar platforms such as Westlaw, Lexis and Office 365. He treats procurement constraints and institutional caution as part of courts’ obligation to get decisions right rather than innovate first.
qs: we certainly don’t have the budgets for legal technologists to come in and build on-prem tools at the moment.
enterprise tools have minimum users and typically the courts can’t afford those minimum user requirements.
it’s the court’s job to get it right. It’s not our job to be first.
now that we’re seeing these tools being built into the tools that we commonly use and trust, you’ll see a greater and greater adoption by the courts, I believe.

kp.k: Sensitive judicial data requires tool-specific security safeguards
kp.d: Schlegel recommends against entering private or sealed material into off-the-shelf LLMs without enterprise protections and remains cautious about sealed records and child sexual abuse material even with enterprise tools. Drawing an analogy with earlier cloud-storage adoption, he recommends appropriate security levels, disabling training on inputs, and understanding tools before deciding what data can safely be used.
qs: don’t put anything that’s secure or private or sealed in these, you know, off the shelf LLMs, unless you have an enterprise level tool.
And even then I would not put CSAM or sealed records necessarily in
Make sure you have the right security levels. Make sure that what you’re putting in there is, you know, safe and secure.

kp.k: Small pilots can build support for process modernization
kp.d: Schlegel recommends starting with one judge and chambers, demonstrating savings and citizen benefits before seeking wider funding. He acknowledges fragmented authority, budgets and political resistance. As an anecdotal example of non-AI process improvement, he describes inexpensive text and email reminders reducing failures to appear and unnecessary motions-to-compel hearings; no formal outcome measurements are supplied.
qs: always start small and start with a pilot. Pick one judge in one chambers, in one jurisdiction
So go change your own chambers.
I can actually send text and email reminders that cut down on failures to appear and actually cut down on silly motions to compel hearings
Oh, that’s only $150 for a year.

kp.k: AI helps Schlegel produce public educational material
kp.d: Schlegel explains that his newsletter and public commentary aim to share ideas for improving the justice system and invite others’ feedback. He reports using AI to produce initial drafts from his own experience-based ideas, followed by approximately 30 minutes of editing. This is a personal example of assisted content production, distinct from his stricter recommendations for judicial decision drafting.
qs: It’s an idea or a thought or a concept that I have based upon my years of experience in the justice system.
I tell whatever tools I’m using, to start the first draft for me.
spent 30 minutes editing it and I send it out.

kp.k: Voice cloning threatens protective-order proceedings and self-represented litigants
kp.d: Schlegel identifies cloned audio in domestic-violence and protective-order proceedings as his immediate concern. His hypothetical scenario involves fabricated threats, authentication by a familiar listener and cautious judicial intervention before effective rebuttal. He stresses that self-represented parties typically lack immediate expert assistance, so later vindication may not repair months without children, housing or firearm access. These are risk arguments, not documented incident counts or measured error rates.
qs: The voice cloning scares the heck out of me.
authentication by a known person makes it admissible.
Most of these things are self-represented litigants, so we’re not going to have experts.
six months of not being able to see my kids or not being able to carry the firearm because you cloned my voice, that’s a long time.

kp.k: Pretrial disclosure should address AI-created and enhanced evidence
kp.d: Schlegel recommends adding disclosure requirements to criminal and civil pretrial orders before legislation requires it. He distinguishes fraudulent fabrication from legitimate enhancement and AI-generated demonstrative exhibits: the purpose is early scrutiny and avoiding trial disruption, not treating every AI use as misconduct.
qs: Start building that into your pre-trial practice, both on criminal and civil.
requiring disclosure of any potential uses of these tools or any concerns that you have of your opponent regarding any evidence that they may have
Sometimes they use AI to enhance evidence and it’s not being done for nefarious reasons.
here’s a demonstrative exhibit that I’ve used gen AI to create. It’s fine, but let’s put it out there first

kp.k: Schlegel describes expanded Louisiana diligence duties for evidence
kp.d: Schlegel reports a Louisiana measure, rendered in the transcript as 'act 2025,' requiring reasonable diligence before offering evidence and pretrial raising of reasonably suspected deepfakes. He contrasts this with a prior prohibition on knowingly offering false evidence and with contemplated federal evidence-rule changes. He recommends basic provenance questions about when photographs were taken, the original phone and subsequent handling; the transcript does not establish the measure’s precise legal citation.
qs: We passed act 2025 that put it on the lawyers and said, look, if you have a reasonable suspicion of deep fake evidence being used by your opponent, bring it up pre-trial.
We modified that to say you must use reasonable diligence before offering evidence
Ask the five to 10 questions that raise your BS meter so that you can then make a reasonable effort.

kp.k: Detection and watermarking cannot presently replace evidentiary scrutiny
kp.d: Reporting what experts have told him rather than claiming technical expertise, Schlegel says available deepfake detectors are insufficiently accurate and provenance markers or watermarks can be removed. He hopes for better detection but currently favors awareness, questioning and pretrial handling over reliance on technical authentication alone.
qs: I’ve been told that there aren’t any deep fake finders that are accurate enough
I’m not an expert, but my appreciation from speaking with them is they can remove the CP2A or a C2PA and take out the watermarks and then recreate the same digital file.
The first step is to be aware.

kp.k: Court technologists could enable deeper operational and accessibility improvements
kp.d: In his explicitly forward-looking answer, Schlegel predicts that funded legal-technologist roles and redesigned case-management systems will matter more than isolated research or drafting tools. He envisages digestible records, shorter timelines, guided public forms, readable materials, multilingual avatar explanations and better juror communications. He frames public-facing assistance as helping people navigate courts, expressly setting unauthorized-practice questions aside; these are proposed capabilities, not demonstrated results.
qs: the biggest crystal ball, if you will, moment will be when courts receive budgets that they can hire a true legal technologist.
the real magic is going to be when we are able to redesign our case management systems
we have the record in a digestible format where we can shrink that six month timeline to six weeks.
you have a name change. Here is the form. Here is a guided form. Here’s how you do it.
can take our forms and make them readable so that everybody can read them and how to do it.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Schlegel predicts that AI's largest judicial impact will come from redesigned court administration and case management, while judicial decisions must remain human.
pts.d: Schlegel envisages AI preparing more digestible records, accelerating proceedings, and improving public-facing court information. His six-month-to-six-week example is an illustrative possibility, not a measured result. He distinguishes assistance with court work from delegation of judicial authority, which he rejects.

pts.k: Schlegel predicts increasing judicial adoption as AI becomes embedded in trusted software, subject to budget, procurement, and security constraints.
pts.d: He identifies integration into established research and office tools as a prerequisite for wide adoption. Enterprise minimum-user requirements and the cost of technical staff constrain courts. He recommends small pilots to demonstrate savings and public benefits before seeking broader funding; these benefits are asserted rather than quantified.

pts.k: Schlegel sees useful drafting assistance for bounded judicial tasks but warns that AI can steer judicial reasoning through confirmation bias.
pts.d: He distinguishes short writ dispositions from lengthy appellate opinions, citing current context-window limitations. He argues that a tool's tendency to reinforce the user's direction can help advocates tighten arguments but can lead judges down an unintended path. For judicial drafting, he recommends supplying the relevant facts, law, and independently determined answer rather than asking AI to derive a first draft from the parties' submissions. Separately, he reports using AI to draft his public articles before human editing.

pts.k: Schlegel warns that cloned voices and other synthetic evidence can produce immediate harmful court outcomes before their falsity can be established.
pts.d: His central example is a hypothetical protective-order proceeding based on a fabricated threatening recording. He argues that familiar-voice authentication and judicial caution could allow such evidence to support restrictions, while later expert investigation comes too late to prevent months of harm. He distinguishes deceptive fabrication from legitimate AI enhancement or demonstrative exhibits and recommends early disclosure and pretrial scrutiny.

pts.k: Schlegel argues that technical detection alone cannot presently resolve synthetic-evidence risks and that lawyers' pretrial diligence is important.
pts.d: He reports expert advice that deepfake detectors are insufficiently reliable and that provenance markers can be removed. He describes a Louisiana change requiring reasonable diligence before offering evidence and pretrial notification of reasonable suspicions about opponents' evidence. He considers these practices more useful than merely modifying evidence rules. The transcript's statutory reference is ambiguous, so no precise act number is inferred.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims primarily rest on Schlegel's judicial experience, personal AI use, guidance work, hypothetical scenarios, and reported expert advice.
pts.d: No controlled studies, model benchmarks, adoption statistics, or quantified court-efficiency results are supplied. His personal article-drafting workflow is an experiential example. He reports positive reader feedback on judicial guidance but explicitly does not claim widespread adoption. The protective-order example is hypothetical, not an identified deepfake case. Detector and watermark claims are attributed to experts he has consulted, with an explicit disclaimer of technical expertise. His examples of inexpensive reminders concern general process technology and should not be treated as measured AI effects.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Schlegel distinguishes present capabilities and risks from conditional future transformation; he provides no firm adoption deadline.
pts.d: The document is labelled 2026, but the interview describes itself as taking place the day after ChatGPT's third anniversary; relative references such as 'today' and 'this year' should therefore not automatically be assigned to 2026. Voice-cloning risks and short-task drafting are described as current. Larger case-management benefits depend on staffing budgets and redesign. Adoption depends on trusted integrations, appropriate security, affordable licensing, and procurement. He cautions against uploading sensitive material into off-the-shelf tools and remains cautious about sealed records even with enterprise tools. His ten-year remark concerns incremental modernization rather than a dated AI forecast.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are judges and clerks, advocates, court administrators, litigants, self-represented court users, and jurors.
pts.d: Judges and clerks may gain drafting and record-processing assistance while retaining responsibility for judgment. Advocates may strengthen arguments but face additional evidence-checking work. Courts need technical capacity and funding. Litigants could benefit from shorter delays but face serious harm from synthetic evidence, especially in protective-order proceedings where expert assistance is often absent. Public-facing AI could improve navigation through guided forms, readable information, multilingual avatars, and jury instructions. Schlegel frames these as information services and expressly sets aside unauthorized-practice questions rather than claiming AI can replace legal representation.
